borders.before: the lecturer's introductory remarks, course context, and lecture learning objectives
borders.after: the core definition of cancer as a genetic, evolutionary disease and the role of the microenvironment
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 1 is introductory framing, while subtopic 2 begins the substantive scientific content of the lecture.
borders.caseForMoving: There is no alternative boundary, as subtopic 1 is purely introductory and subtopic 2 directly introduces the biology of cancer.
borders.caseForRemoving: Removing the border would conflate administrative course framing with the substantive scientific teaching on cancer etiology.

borders.before: epidemiological geographic patterns and the debate over genetic versus environmental and bad luck causes
borders.after: infectious agents and pathogens that drive carcinogenesis, such as H. pylori, viruses, and parasites
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 7 begins a focused exploration of specific biological carcinogens (pathogens), moving on from the general epidemiological and conceptual framework in subtopics 2–6.
borders.caseForMoving: Moving the border to subtopic 6 would place general global epidemiology with infectious mechanisms; moving it to subtopic 8 would separate the general survey of infectious agents from the Burkitt lymphoma case study.
borders.caseForRemoving: Removing the border would blend the overarching discussion of cancer causation and epidemiology with detailed pathogen mechanisms.

borders.before: a detailed case study of Epstein-Barr virus, malaria, and chromosomal translocation in Burkitt lymphoma
borders.after: dietary, physical, and chemical mutagens, beginning with aflatoxin epoxide adduct formation
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 9 shifts the lecture from biological agents (pathogens) to chemical and physical mutagens that damage DNA directly or via metabolic activation.
borders.caseForMoving: Moving the border to subtopic 8 would split the infectious agents section in half; moving it to subtopic 10 would omit aflatoxin from the chemical mutagen section.
borders.caseForRemoving: Removing the border would merge pathogen-driven carcinogenesis with chemical and radiation-induced DNA damage mechanisms.

borders.before: chemical mutagens requiring xenobiotic metabolic activation and tissue-specific activation of beta-naphthylamine
borders.after: non-mutagenic tumour promotion, chronic inflammation illustrated by asbestos, and the Berenbaum initiator-promoter model
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 14 introduces the fundamental conceptual distinction between tumour initiators (mutagens) and tumour promoters (inflammatory/proliferative stimuli).
borders.caseForMoving: Moving the border to subtopic 13 would place beta-naphthylamine (a direct/metabolically activated mutagen) into the promotion topic; moving it to subtopic 15 would separate the asbestos case study from the promoter concept it exemplifies.
borders.caseForRemoving: Removing the border would conflate direct chemical mutagens with non-mutagenic promoters and host microenvironmental factors.

borders.before: a comprehensive summary of DNA damage mechanisms, xenobiotic metabolism, promoters, and host developmental susceptibility
borders.after: technological and analytical methods used to identify carcinogen exposure, starting with mutational signatures from whole genome sequencing
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 18 transitions from the biological mechanisms of carcinogenesis to the experimental and epidemiological methods used to detect and prove carcinogenicity.
borders.caseForMoving: Moving the border to subtopic 17 would pull a summary slide of mechanisms into the methodology section; moving it to subtopic 19 would separate mutational signatures from other testing methods.
borders.caseForRemoving: Removing the border would combine the biological mechanisms of cancer formation with the diagnostic and experimental methodologies used to study them.

borders.before: in vitro mutagenicity testing using the Ames test and its strengths and limitations compared to in vivo systems
borders.after: lecture wrap-up, real-world risk versus benefit trade-offs regarding carcinogen exposures, and closing remarks
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 22 represents the closing framing and takeaway summary of the lecture, distinct from the technical discussion of carcinogenicity assays.
borders.caseForMoving: There is no later subtopic, and moving it to subtopic 21 would pull technical Ames test mechanics into the closing remarks.
borders.caseForRemoving: Removing the border would merge the closing framing and concluding thoughts with the technical methodology section.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 2–3 address the fundamental biology of cancer as an evolutionary/genetic disease, whereas subtopics 4–6 focus on environmental exposures, the public debate on 'bad luck', and geographic epidemiology.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 2–6 together build the introductory conceptual framework of cancer etiology, establishing the interplay between intrinsic cellular errors, environmental mutagens, and population-level epidemiological evidence.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopic 7 provides an overview of various oncogenic pathogens, whereas subtopic 8 is a dedicated historical and mechanistic case study of Burkitt lymphoma.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopic 8 serves as the primary detailed example illustrating the viral and co-infectious principles introduced in subtopic 7.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 9–10 discuss aflatoxin and UV light, while subtopics 11–13 focus specifically on polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, xenobiotic metabolism via AhR/CYP1A1, and tissue-specific activation.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: All subtopics in this section systematically address chemical and physical agents that cause DNA damage, bulky adducts, and transversions.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 14–15 define promoters and the Berenbaum model, while subtopics 16–17 focus on host developmental stages, tissue susceptibility, and an overarching summary of mechanisms.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: These subtopics together address the non-initiating factors in carcinogenesis—including chronic inflammation, promoter signalling, host developmental windows, and tissue context.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 18–19 cover human-focused observational methods (mutational signatures and biobank epidemiology), while subtopics 20–21 cover experimental toxicology (in vivo animal bioassays and in vitro Ames tests).
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: All four subtopics form a cohesive survey of the complementary methodological tools used by toxicologists and cancer researchers to prove carcinogenicity.

topics.label: Course Introduction and Learning Objectives
topics.groupedBecause: It provides introductory framing by introducing the lecturer, setting the lecture series context, and outlining the core learning objectives.

topics.label: Cancer Etiology: Genetic, Endogenous, and Environmental Factors
topics.groupedBecause: It establishes the conceptual foundation of cancer as a multi-step genetic disease driven by a balance of intrinsic replication errors, inherited predisposition, and environmental exposures.

topics.label: Infectious Agents and Pathogen-Driven Carcinogenesis
topics.groupedBecause: It examines how oncogenic viruses, bacteria, and parasites contribute to malignancy, featuring an in-depth case study of Burkitt lymphoma.

topics.label: Mechanisms of Chemical and Physical DNA Damage
topics.groupedBecause: It details how dietary, environmental, and chemical carcinogens undergo metabolic activation to induce DNA adducts and specific mutational transitions.

topics.label: Tumour Initiation, Promotion, and Host Susceptibility
topics.groupedBecause: It explores the distinction between mutational tumour initiators and non-mutagenic promoters alongside the influence of inflammation and host developmental timing on carcinogenesis.

topics.label: Methodologies for Detecting and Proving Carcinogenicity
topics.groupedBecause: It reviews the analytical, epidemiological, in vivo, and in vitro experimental strategies used to evaluate and confirm the carcinogenic potential of agents.

topics.label: Lecture Conclusion and Risk-Benefit Considerations
topics.groupedBecause: It closes the lecture with a summary of environmental causation and frames exposure choices within everyday risk-benefit assessments.
